leftItems.text: SI unit of volume flow rate
SI unit of mass flow rate

A.explain: Each SI unit follows from the defining formula. Dynamic viscosity η is shear stress divided by velocity gradient, so it is pressure times time, Pa·s (= N·s/m² = kg·m⁻¹·s⁻¹). Surface tension is force per unit length, T = F/L, so N/m (= J/m²), while pressure is force per unit area, P = F/A, so the pascal, Pa = N/m². Force itself, F = ma, is the newton, N = kg·m/s², and density, ρ = m/V, is kg/m³. Volume flow rate, written here \(Q_V = A v\) (area times speed), is m³/s, and mass flow rate Q = ρAv, mass per time, is kg/s, so the two flow rates differ by the density factor; check the unit to tell which flow rate is meant. kg·m/s is momentum, not any of these.

A.q: Match each quantity, in the stated unit system, to its unit.

leftItems.text: CGS unit of volume flow rate
CGS unit of mass flow rate

A.explain: CGS units are built from the centimetre, gram and second. The dyne is the force that gives 1 g an acceleration of 1 cm/s², so 1 dyne = 1 g·cm/s² = 10⁻⁵ N. Dynamic viscosity is measured in poise, 1 P = 1 g·cm⁻¹·s⁻¹ = 1 dyne·s/cm² = 0.1 Pa·s; the stokes (1 St = 1 cm²/s) is instead the unit of kinematic viscosity, ν = η/ρ, so it is not the answer for dynamic viscosity. Surface tension is force per length, dyne/cm (= 10⁻³ N/m), while pressure is force per area, dyne/cm² (= 0.1 Pa). Density is g/cm³ (1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³; water is about 1 g/cm³), volume flow rate is cm³/s (= 10⁻⁶ m³/s) and mass flow rate is g/s (= 10⁻³ kg/s).

bernoulli.title: Bernoulli's equation
bernoulli.definition: For an ideal fluid (steady, incompressible, non-viscous, streamline flow), the total mechanical energy per unit volume stays constant: pressure energy + kinetic energy + potential energy = constant. As fluid velocity increases, fluid pressure decreases, and vice versa.
bernoulli.equation:
P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant
P₁ + ½ρv₁² + ρgh₁ = P₂ + ½ρv₂² + ρgh₂
symbols: g = acceleration due to gravity, 9.8 m/s²
h = height above a reference level (m)
uses: Blood flow through arteries and heart valves

diagram.label: Bernoulli along a rising pipe: pressure, kinetic and potential energy per volume add to the same total

poiseuille.title: Poiseuille's law
poiseuille.definition: Poiseuille's law describes the flow of a viscous fluid through a cylindrical tube: the volume flow rate is proportional to the fourth power of the radius and to the pressure difference, and inversely proportional to the viscosity and the length of the tube.
poiseuille.equation: Q = π r⁴ ΔP / (8 η L)
symbols: ΔP = pressure difference between the two ends (Pa)
uses: Blood circulation through arteries and veins

diagram.label: Poiseuille flow through a tube of radius R and length L, and how halving R cuts the flow to one sixteenth

laplace.title: Laplace's law
laplace.definition: Laplace's law links the pressure inside a vessel, its radius, and the tension in its wall: wall tension increases directly with pressure and radius.
laplace.equation:
T = P × r
σ = P r / t
uses: Aneurysm: a bulge with a larger radius carries more wall tension

diagram.label: Laplace law in a vessel: wall tension grows with pressure and radius; an aneurysm bulges out on one side of the wall with a much larger radius

reynolds.title: Reynolds number
reynolds.definition: The Reynolds number, Re, compares inertial force to viscous force and tells you the type of flow: below 2000 laminar (streamline), above 2000 turbulent. Re has no units.
reynolds.equation:
Re = inertial force / viscous force
Re = ρ v D / η
uses: Type of blood flow in an artery

diagram.label: Reynolds number scale: below 2000 laminar, above 2000 turbulent

continuity.title: Equation of continuity
continuity.definition: If no fluid is added or removed between two sections of a tube, flow rate is conserved. For an incompressible fluid such as blood, a narrower area means a larger speed so that A₁v₁ = A₂v₂.
uses: Faster blood flow at a stenosis

diagram.label: Continuity: narrower tube means faster flow; pressure drops as shown by the columns

snell.title: Snell's law
snell.definition: When light crosses the boundary between two media it changes direction (refraction); the product of the index and the sine of the angle from the normal stays the same across the boundary. Going into a higher n the ray bends toward the normal; into a lower n, away from it.
snell.equation: n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂
symbols: n₁, n₂ = refractive indices of the two media
θ₁ = angle of incidence, from the normal
θ₂ = angle of refraction, from the normal

diagram.label: Refraction: entering a higher-index medium the ray bends toward the normal; leaving it, away from the normal

tir.title: Total internal reflection
tir.definition: If the angle of incidence is greater than the critical angle, no light gets out: the ray reflects back into the denser medium. Two conditions: light travels from higher n to lower n, and the angle of incidence is greater than θc.
uses: Mirages and the sparkle of diamonds

diagram.label: Total internal reflection: below, at and above the critical angle

doppler.title: Doppler effect
doppler.definition: The Doppler effect is the change in the frequency, an increase or a decrease, of sound, light or other waves when the source and the observer move towards or away from each other.
symbols: v = speed of sound in air

diagram.label: Doppler effect: a moving source bunches wavefronts ahead, giving a higher pitch, and spreads them behind, giving a lower pitch

refractiveIndex.title: Index of refraction
refractiveIndex.definition: The index of refraction, also called the refractive index, compares the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium. n ≥ 1 and has no units; higher n means slower light.
symbols: c = speed of light in vacuum = 3 × 10⁸ m/s
v = speed of light in the medium

diagram.label: Refraction: entering a higher-index medium the ray bends toward the normal; leaving it, away from the normal

criticalAngle.title: Critical angle
criticalAngle.definition: The critical angle, θc, is the angle of incidence (going from a denser to a rarer medium) at which the angle of refraction becomes 90°, so the refracted ray skims along the surface.
criticalAngle.equation:
n₁ sin θc = n₂ sin 90°
sin θc = n₂ / n₁   (n₁ > n₂)

diagram.label: Total internal reflection: below, at and above the critical angle

surfaceTension.title: Surface tension
surfaceTension.definition: Surface tension is the property of a liquid surface that makes it behave like a stretched elastic membrane; it is the force acting per unit length along the surface of a liquid, from cohesive forces between liquid molecules.

diagram.label: Surface tension from unbalanced pulls on surface molecules, and capillary rise of water and fall of mercury

viscosity.title: Viscosity
viscosity.definition: Viscosity (η) is the resistance of a fluid to shear deformation or flow, caused by internal friction between adjacent fluid layers.
viscosity.equation:
F = η A v / y
F / A = η × (v / y)
uses: Polycythemia and anemia change blood viscosity

diagram.label: Viscosity: a force F drags the top plate at speed v over a fluid layer of thickness y; layers move slower near the fixed plate

viscosity.title: Viscosity
points: ### Units of viscosity, step by step

Start from the defining relation for the two-plate picture: the viscous force is \(F = \eta A v / y\), so \(\eta = \dfrac{F}{A}\cdot\dfrac{y}{v}\). Here \(F/A\) is the shear stress and \(v/y\) is the **velocity gradient** (how fast the speed changes across the layers).
1. Shear stress \(F/A\) is a force per area: newtons per square metre, **N/m²**, which has its own name, the **pascal (Pa)**.
2. The velocity gradient \(v/y\) is (m/s) ÷ m = **1/s**, so dividing by it multiplies by seconds.
3. So \(\eta\) has unit **Pa × s = Pa·s**, the *pascal-second*. Written with the newton instead of the pascal (1 Pa = 1 N/m²) it is **N·s/m²** (also N·s·m⁻²).
4. Writing the newton in SI base units (1 N = 1 kg·m/s²): N·s/m² = (kg·m/s²)·s/m² = **kg/(m·s)**, also written kg·m⁻¹·s⁻¹.

These are **not three different units**: SI has one unit of viscosity, and Pa·s, N·s/m² and kg/(m·s) are the same unit written with a named derived unit (Pa), with another derived unit (N), or only with the base units kg, m and s. Pa·s is the usual name. When the denominator has two units, keep them together: kg/(m·s) means kg ÷ (m × s). Typed without brackets, *kg/m·s* is read the same way here as a shorthand, but kg·s/m would be a different, wrong dimension.

**CGS comparison:** the CGS unit is the **poise (P)**, 1 P = 1 g/(cm·s) = 1 dyne·s/cm². Since 1 g = 10⁻³ kg and 1 cm = 10⁻² m, 1 P = 10⁻³ kg / (10⁻² m · s) = **0.1 Pa·s**, so **1 Pa·s = 10 P**. Water at about 20 °C is close to 1 × 10⁻³ Pa·s = 1 centipoise (cP).
**Dynamic vs kinematic viscosity:** η (this lesson) is *dynamic* viscosity. Kinematic viscosity is \(\nu = \eta/\rho\), in m²/s (CGS: the stokes, 1 St = 1 cm²/s); it is a different quantity.

exam.q: Define viscosity.
exam.a: Viscosity is the internal friction of a fluid: its resistance to flow, or to shear deformation, caused by the friction between adjacent layers moving at different speeds. Its SI unit is the pascal-second (Pa·s) and its CGS unit is the poise (P), with 1 P = 0.1 Pa·s.

exam.q: Why can the SI unit of viscosity be written as Pa·s, N·s/m² and kg/(m·s)?
exam.a: Because η = (F/A)·(y/v): F/A is a pressure in N/m² = Pa and y/v is a time in s, so η is in Pa·s. Replacing Pa by N/m² gives N·s/m², and replacing N by kg·m/s² gives kg/(m·s). They are one unit written with different named units.

exam.q: How does viscosity relate to the viscous force and to flow in a tube?
exam.a: The viscous force is F = ηAv/y, so F ∝ η for the same area A and velocity gradient v/y. In a tube, Poiseuille's law Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL) gives Q ∝ 1/η: doubling the viscosity (for example in polycythemia) halves the flow for the same pressure difference, radius and length.

bernoulli.title: Bernoulli's equation and its medical uses

exam.q: State Bernoulli's principle.
exam.a: For an ideal (incompressible, non-viscous) fluid in steady streamline flow, the sum of the pressure, the kinetic energy per unit volume and the potential energy per unit volume is constant along a streamline: P + ½ρv² + ρgh = constant. Where the fluid moves faster, its pressure is lower.

exam.q: Why does a Venturi mask draw in room air?
exam.a: Oxygen is forced through a narrow opening, so its speed rises; by Bernoulli's principle its pressure drops below the surrounding air pressure, and that pressure difference pulls in (entrains) a fixed ratio of room air, giving a controlled oxygen concentration.

exam.q: How are speed and pressure related in Bernoulli's equation at the same height?
exam.a: With h constant, P + ½ρv² = constant, so a rise in speed gives a fall in pressure: P₁ − P₂ = ½ρ(v₂² − v₁²). The pressure drop grows with the square of the speed, which is why Doppler echocardiography can estimate a valve pressure gradient from the measured blood speed.

continuity.title: Flow rates and the equation of continuity
points: **Naming the two flow rates:** the course writes **mass flow rate** as \(Q = \rho A v\) (also written ṁ), in kg/s, and **volume flow rate** as \(A v\), in m³/s. In this lesson the volume flow rate is labelled \(Q_V = A v\) to keep the two apart; they are linked by \(Q = \rho\,Q_V\).

**Units from the formula:** \(\rho A v\) → (kg/m³)·(m²)·(m/s) = kg/s; \(A v\) → m²·(m/s) = m³/s. In CGS the same steps give g/s and cm³/s (1 g/s = 10⁻³ kg/s, 1 cm³/s = 10⁻⁶ m³/s); neither has a special named unit.

notes.heading: ## 4. Mass flow rate & volume flow rate

exam.q: State the equation of continuity.
exam.a: For a steady flow of an incompressible fluid (constant density) through a tube, the volume passing any cross-section per second is the same everywhere: A₁v₁ = A₂v₂. It follows from conservation of mass, ρA₁v₁ = ρA₂v₂.

exam.q: Why does blood speed up at a stenosis?
exam.a: The same volume of blood must pass every cross-section each second (continuity). At the narrowing the area A is smaller, so the speed v must be larger to keep A v constant.

exam.q: How are mass flow rate and volume flow rate related?
exam.a: Mass flow rate is Q = ρAv in kg/s; volume flow rate is Av in m³/s. They differ by the density: mass flow rate = ρ × volume flow rate. For a fixed flow, v ∝ 1/A, so halving the area doubles the speed.

exam.q: State Poiseuille's law.
exam.a: For steady laminar flow of a viscous fluid through a cylindrical tube, the volume flow rate is Q = πr⁴ΔP/(8ηL), where r is the radius, ΔP the pressure difference between the ends, η the viscosity and L the length.

exam.q: Why does a small narrowing of a vessel cause a large drop in flow?
exam.a: Flow depends on the fourth power of the radius, Q ∝ r⁴, so halving the radius reduces the flow to 1/16 of its value for the same pressure difference; resistance rises in the same proportion.

exam.q: How does flow depend on each quantity in Poiseuille's law?
exam.a: Q ∝ r⁴, Q ∝ ΔP, Q ∝ 1/η and Q ∝ 1/L. Wider, shorter tubes, a bigger pressure difference and a less viscous fluid all increase flow, which is why IV infusion sets use the cannula size and bag height to control the rate.

notes.heading: ## 5. Applications of Bernoulli and Poiseuille: TIA

exam.q: Define a transient ischemic attack (TIA).
exam.a: A TIA is a temporary lack of blood supply to part of the brain, often caused by narrowing of a neck (carotid) artery, which produces short-lived stroke-like symptoms.

exam.q: Why can a narrowed carotid artery cause a TIA?
exam.a: At the narrowing the blood speeds up (continuity), its pressure falls (Bernoulli), and the much higher resistance of the narrow segment sharply reduces flow (Poiseuille, Q ∝ r⁴), so the brain temporarily receives too little blood.

exam.q: How do continuity, Bernoulli and Poiseuille link in a stenosis?
exam.a: Smaller area → higher speed (A₁v₁ = A₂v₂) → lower pressure (P + ½ρv² constant) → smaller radius → much lower flow (Q ∝ r⁴). Each law explains one step of the chain.

notes.heading: ## 6. Laplace's law — tension in vessel walls

exam.q: State Laplace's law for a cylindrical vessel.
exam.a: The tension in the wall of a cylindrical vessel is proportional to the pressure inside it and to its radius: T = P r (for a sphere, T = P r / 2).

exam.q: Why is an aneurysm at risk of rupture as it enlarges?
exam.a: By Laplace's law the wall tension is T = P r, so as the aneurysm bulges and its radius grows much larger than the normal radius, the tension in its wall rises a lot for the same blood pressure; the wall stress σ = P r / t rises too, weakening the wall and making rupture more likely.

exam.q: How do wall tension, pressure and radius relate?
exam.a: T ∝ P at a fixed radius and T ∝ r at a fixed pressure: doubling the radius doubles the wall tension. Dividing by the wall thickness gives the wall stress, σ = P r / t. For a sphere such as an alveolus, T = P r / 2, the same as P = 2T / r.

exam.q: Define streamline (laminar) flow.
exam.a: Streamline or laminar flow is smooth, orderly flow in which the fluid moves in parallel layers; in a vessel the speed is highest in the centre and lowest at the wall, giving a roughly parabolic velocity profile.

exam.q: Why does turbulent flow through a narrowed valve produce a murmur?
exam.a: Above a certain speed, or at an irregular or sudden narrowing, the layers break up into swirls and eddies; this disordered flow vibrates the surrounding tissue and produces the audible sound heard as a heart murmur.

exam.q: How is the type of flow related to speed and vessel shape?
exam.a: Higher speed, larger diameter and irregular or suddenly narrowed vessels push flow from laminar towards turbulent; turbulence increases energy loss and resistance. The Reynolds number Re = ρvD/η measures this tendency.

exam.q: Define the Reynolds number.
exam.a: The Reynolds number is a dimensionless number that compares inertial forces to viscous forces in a flowing fluid, Re = ρvD/η, and tells whether the flow is laminar or turbulent.

exam.q: Why does a high Reynolds number mean turbulent flow?
exam.a: Re is inertia ÷ viscosity. When Re is high, the fluid's momentum (ρvD) dominates the internal friction (η) that keeps the layers ordered, so disturbances grow into swirls and eddies.

exam.q: How does the Reynolds number depend on its variables, and what are the limits?
exam.a: Re ∝ ρ, Re ∝ v, Re ∝ D and Re ∝ 1/η. Below about 2000 the flow is laminar; above about 2000 it tends to become turbulent. Re has no units.

surfaceTension.title: Surface tension, capillarity and surfactant
points: ### Units of surface tension, step by step

Surface tension is force per length, \(T = F/L\): N ÷ m = **N/m**. Multiplying top and bottom by metres gives N·m/m² = **J/m²**, so it is also surface energy per area. In base units, (kg·m/s²)/m = **kg/s²**. All three are the same SI unit.
**CGS:** dyne ÷ cm = **dyne/cm** (= erg/cm²). Since 1 dyne = 10⁻⁵ N and 1 cm = 10⁻² m, 1 dyne/cm = 10⁻⁵/10⁻² N/m = **10⁻³ N/m**; water ≈ 0.072 N/m ≈ 72 dyne/cm.
### Water and mercury in glass: cause before effect
1. **Cause:** compare adhesion (liquid–glass attraction) with cohesion (liquid–liquid attraction). Water: adhesion wins. Mercury: cohesion wins.
2. **Contact angle θ** follows from that balance: water wets clean glass, θ < 90°; mercury does not wet it, θ > 90°.
3. **Meniscus:** θ < 90° curves the surface up at the walls (concave, water); θ > 90° bulges it up in the middle (convex, mercury).

4. **Rise or fall:** in \(h = 2\gamma\cos\theta/(\rho g r)\), cos θ > 0 for water so h > 0 (rises); cos θ < 0 for mercury so h < 0 (falls). Surface tension γ, density ρ and radius r set **how far**, not which way: mercury's large γ and large ρ change the size of the drop, and a narrower tube gives a bigger rise or fall.

exam.q: Define surface tension.
exam.a: Surface tension is the property of a liquid surface that makes it behave like a stretched elastic membrane, due to cohesive forces between the liquid molecules. It is the force per unit length acting along the surface, T = F/L, with SI unit N/m (= J/m²) and CGS unit dyne/cm (1 dyne/cm = 10⁻³ N/m).

exam.q: Why does water rise in a glass capillary while mercury falls?
exam.a: Water's adhesion to glass is stronger than its cohesion, so it wets the glass (contact angle below 90°), forms a concave meniscus and cos θ > 0 makes it rise. Mercury's cohesion is stronger than its adhesion, so it does not wet the glass (contact angle above 90°), forms a convex meniscus and cos θ < 0 makes it fall.

exam.q: How does capillary height depend on the tube and the liquid?
exam.a: h = 2γ cos θ/(ρ g r): h ∝ γ, h ∝ 1/ρ and h ∝ 1/r, while the sign of cos θ sets the direction. A narrower tube gives a larger rise (or fall). For alveoli, P = 2T/r: surfactant lowers T so less pressure keeps small alveoli open.

exam.q: Define the Doppler effect.
exam.a: The Doppler effect is the change in the observed frequency of a wave when the source and the observer move relative to each other: the frequency rises when they approach and falls when they move apart.

exam.q: Why can Doppler ultrasound measure blood speed?
exam.a: Moving red blood cells reflect the ultrasound; because they move relative to the probe, the reflected frequency is shifted, and the size of the shift depends on the blood speed, so measuring the shift gives the speed (as in Doppler echocardiography and the detection of DVT).

exam.q: How is the frequency shift related to motion?
exam.a: The shift grows with the relative speed: approach raises the observed frequency, recession lowers it, and with no relative motion there is no shift. The size of the shift is set by the speeds of the source and observer compared with the speed of the wave.

reflection.title: Reflection, the normal and real vs virtual images

exam.q: Define the normal in reflection.
exam.a: The normal is an imaginary line at 90° to the reflecting surface at the point where the ray strikes it; the angles of incidence and reflection are measured from the normal, not from the surface.

exam.q: Why is the image in a plane mirror virtual?
exam.a: The reflected rays do not actually meet behind the mirror; they only appear to come from a point behind it when traced backwards, so no light passes through the image and it cannot be caught on a screen.

exam.q: How are the incident ray, reflected ray and normal related?
exam.a: They lie in the same plane, the incident and reflected rays are on opposite sides of the normal, and the angle of incidence equals the angle of reflection, θi = θr. For a plane mirror the image distance equals the object distance.

sphericalMirrors.title: Spherical mirrors: pole, centre, focus and images
points: **The pole (P)**, also called the vertex, is the **centre point of the mirror's reflecting surface**. It is a point *on* the mirror. Do not confuse it with the **centre of curvature (C)**, the centre of the sphere the mirror is cut from, which lies off the mirror at a distance r (the radius of curvature).
**The principal axis** is the straight line through **P and C**. The **focus (F)** lies on it, halfway between P and C, so f = r/2.

**P is the reference point for distances:** the focal length f, the radius of curvature r, the object distance \(d_o\) and the image distance \(d_i\) are all measured **from the pole** along the principal axis.

**The normal at the pole:** the normal at any point of a spherical mirror lies along the radius through C, so at P the normal is the principal axis itself. A ray hitting P therefore reflects at the same angle on the other side of the axis.

**Signs (mirror equation 1/f = 1/\(d_o\) + 1/\(d_i\)):** f is positive for a concave (converging) mirror and negative for a convex (diverging) mirror; \(d_i\) is positive for a real image and negative for a virtual image.

exam.q: Define the pole of a spherical mirror.
exam.a: The pole (P), or vertex, is the centre point of the mirror's reflecting surface. It lies on the mirror and on the principal axis, and it is the point from which the focal length, radius of curvature, object distance and image distance are measured.

exam.q: Why is the pole different from the centre of curvature?
exam.a: The pole is a point on the mirror surface, while the centre of curvature (C) is the centre of the sphere the mirror is part of, a distance r away from the mirror; the principal axis joins the two, and the focus F lies halfway between them.

exam.q: How are the pole, focus and centre of curvature related?
exam.a: They all lie on the principal axis, with PF = f and PC = r, and f = r/2 (r = 2f). A concave mirror has a real focus in front of it (f positive); a convex mirror has a virtual focus behind it (f negative).

exam.q: Define the refractive index (index of refraction).
exam.a: The refractive index of a medium is the ratio of the speed of light in vacuum to its speed in the medium, n = c/v. It has no units and is at least 1 (exactly 1 in vacuum).

exam.q: Why is the refractive index never less than 1?
exam.a: Light travels fastest in vacuum, so its speed v in any medium is at most c; since n = c/v, n is at least 1.

exam.q: How is refractive index related to the speed of light and optical density?
exam.a: n ∝ 1/v: a higher n means slower light and an optically denser medium (water n ≈ 1.33, crown glass ≈ 1.52, diamond ≈ 2.42). It enters Snell's law, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂.

exam.q: State Snell's law.
exam.a: When light passes from one medium into another, n₁ sin θ₁ = n₂ sin θ₂, where n₁ and n₂ are the refractive indices and θ₁ and θ₂ are the angles of incidence and refraction measured from the normal.

exam.q: Why does light bend towards the normal when it enters a denser medium?
exam.a: It slows down in the medium with the higher refractive index; with n₂ > n₁, Snell's law gives sin θ₂ < sin θ₁, so the refracted ray makes a smaller angle with the normal.

exam.q: How are the angles and refractive indices related?
exam.a: sin θ₁ / sin θ₂ = n₂ / n₁ = v₁ / v₂. A ray along the normal (θ₁ = 0) is not bent; going from denser to rarer the ray bends away from the normal, which leads to the critical angle.

tir.title: Critical angle and total internal reflection

exam.q: Define the critical angle.
exam.a: The critical angle is the angle of incidence in the optically denser medium for which the angle of refraction into the rarer medium is 90° to the normal, so the refracted ray travels along the boundary.

exam.q: Why does total internal reflection happen only from a denser to a rarer medium?
exam.a: Only then does the refracted ray bend away from the normal, reaching 90° at the critical angle; beyond it no refraction is possible and all the light is reflected back into the denser medium. From rarer to denser the ray bends towards the normal and can always refract.

exam.q: How is the critical angle related to the refractive indices?
exam.a: From Snell's law with θ₂ = 90°, sin θc = n₂/n₁ (for n₁ > n₂); into air, sin θc = 1/n. A larger n gives a smaller critical angle. TIR (used in optical fibres and endoscopes) needs incidence greater than θc.

lenses.title: Lenses and lens power
points: A **convex (converging) lens** brings parallel rays together at a real focus on the far side and has **positive** power; a **concave (diverging) lens** spreads them as if from a virtual focus on the incoming side and has **negative** power. Power is \(P = 1/f\) with f in metres; its unit, the **dioptre (D)**, is the same as m⁻¹ (no separate CGS name).

exam.q: Define the power of a lens.
exam.a: The power of a lens is the reciprocal of its focal length in metres, P = 1/f, measured in dioptres (D); 1 D = 1 m⁻¹. Convex lenses have positive power and concave lenses negative power.

exam.q: Why is a concave lens called diverging?
exam.a: It refracts parallel rays so that they spread out, and they only appear to come from a virtual focus on the incoming side; a convex lens instead brings parallel rays to a real focus.

exam.q: How do focal length and power relate, and how do lenses combine?
exam.a: P = 1/f, so a shorter focal length means a stronger lens (f = 0.5 m → 2 D). For thin lenses in contact the powers add, P = P₁ + P₂, which is how a corrective lens adds to the eye's power.

eye.title: The human eye, accommodation, near and far point

exam.q: Define accommodation.
exam.a: Accommodation is the process by which the ciliary muscles change the shape, and so the focal length, of the eye's lens so that objects at different distances are focused on the retina.

exam.q: Why does the cornea do most of the focusing?
exam.a: Light bends most where the change in refractive index is largest, at the air–cornea boundary, giving the cornea about 43 dioptres; the lens adds a smaller, adjustable amount (about 17–20 D) through accommodation.

exam.q: How are the near point and far point related to accommodation?
exam.a: The near point is the closest distance at which the eye can focus clearly, using maximum accommodation (about 25 cm for a normal adult eye); the far point is the farthest, with the lens relaxed (infinity for a normal eye). Loss of accommodation moves the near point farther away.

exam.q: Define myopia.
exam.a: Myopia (near-sightedness) is a vision defect in which near objects are seen clearly but distant objects are blurred, because the image of a distant object forms in front of the retina; it is corrected with a diverging (concave) lens.

exam.q: Why does a concave lens correct myopia while a convex lens corrects hyperopia?
exam.a: A myopic eye converges light too strongly, so a diverging lens with negative power spreads the rays slightly before they enter the eye; a hyperopic eye converges too weakly, so a converging lens with positive power adds the missing focusing.

exam.q: How are the four defects related to their causes and corrections?
exam.a: Myopia: image in front of the retina → concave lens. Hyperopia: image behind the retina → convex lens. Presbyopia: age-related loss of accommodation → convex (reading) lenses. Astigmatism: irregular corneal curvature → cylindrical lens.

exam.q: Define a laser.
exam.a: LASER stands for Light Amplification by Stimulated Emission of Radiation: a device in which an active medium, pumped by an energy source and placed in an optical cavity, amplifies light by stimulated emission to give a monochromatic, coherent, highly directional and intense beam.

exam.q: Why can a laser act as a bloodless knife in microsurgery?
exam.a: Its beam can be focused to a very small spot of high intensity that cuts tissue precisely while the heat seals (coagulates) small blood vessels, so there is little bleeding.

exam.q: How do the parts of a laser relate to its light?
exam.a: The pump supplies energy to the active medium, the active medium produces light by stimulated emission, and the mirrors of the optical cavity bounce it back and forth to amplify it before part leaves as the beam. In LASIK this precision is used to reshape the cornea for myopia and hyperopia.

units.title: SI and CGS units built from the formulas
points: **Base and derived units.** SI has base units such as the metre (m), kilogram (kg) and second (s); CGS uses the centimetre, gram and second. Every other unit is **derived** by putting the base units through the defining formula, and some derived units get their own names (newton, pascal; dyne, poise). That is why one quantity can be written several ways: Pa·s, N·s/m² and kg/(m·s) are the same SI unit.

| Quantity | Formula | SI unit | CGS unit | Link |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Force | F = m a | N = kg·m/s² | dyne = g·cm/s² | 1 dyne = 10⁻⁵ N |
| Pressure | P = F / A | Pa = N/m² | dyne/cm² | 1 dyne/cm² = 0.1 Pa |
| Density | ρ = m / V | kg/m³ | g/cm³ | 1 g/cm³ = 1000 kg/m³ |
| Dynamic viscosity | η = (F/A)·(y/v) | Pa·s = kg/(m·s) | poise, P = g/(cm·s) | 1 P = 0.1 Pa·s |
| Surface tension | T = F / L | N/m = J/m² | dyne/cm | 1 dyne/cm = 10⁻³ N/m |
| Mass flow rate | Q = ρ A v | kg/s | g/s | 1 g/s = 10⁻³ kg/s |
| Volume flow rate | \(Q_V = A v\) | m³/s | cm³/s | 1 cm³/s = 10⁻⁶ m³/s |

**Working one out:** pressure is force ÷ area, so in CGS it is dyne ÷ cm² = dyne/cm²; converting, 10⁻⁵ N ÷ 10⁻⁴ m² = 0.1 N/m² = 0.1 Pa. Viscosity is pressure × time (shear stress ÷ velocity gradient), so CGS gives dyne·s/cm², which is the poise.

**Common confusions:** pressure (N/m²) and surface tension (N/m) differ by one metre: area vs length. Mass flow (kg/s) and volume flow (m³/s) differ by the density. The **stokes** (cm²/s) is the CGS unit of *kinematic* viscosity ν = η/ρ, not of dynamic viscosity. kg·m/s is momentum. Refractive index and Reynolds number are ratios with no unit, and lens power in dioptres is simply m⁻¹.

exam.q: Define a derived unit, using viscosity as an example.
exam.a: A derived unit is built from base units through the formula that defines the quantity. Viscosity η = (F/A)·(y/v) gives Pa·s in SI (= N·s/m² = kg/(m·s)) and the poise in CGS (= g/(cm·s)), with 1 P = 0.1 Pa·s.

exam.q: Why are N/m and N/m² not the same unit?
exam.a: N/m is force per length (surface tension) while N/m² is force per area (pressure, the pascal); they differ by a factor of one metre, so they measure different quantities.

exam.q: How does a unit conversion follow from the base units?
exam.a: Replace each base unit: for pressure, 1 dyne/cm² = 10⁻⁵ N ÷ 10⁻⁴ m² = 0.1 Pa; for density, 1 g/cm³ = 10⁻³ kg ÷ 10⁻⁶ m³ = 1000 kg/m³; for mass flow, 1 g/s = 10⁻³ kg/s.

waves.title: Waves: types, parts and v = λf

exam.q: Define wavelength and amplitude.
exam.a: Wavelength (λ) is the length of one cycle: the distance between two neighbouring identical points of a wave, such as crest to crest. Amplitude (A) is the height of the wave above its rest position, the undisturbed state.

exam.q: Why can sound not travel through a vacuum, while light can?
exam.a: Sound is a mechanical, longitudinal wave: it is passed on by particles of a medium pushing their neighbours, making compressions and rarefactions. A vacuum has no particles to do this. Light is an electromagnetic wave, which needs no medium and travels through vacuum at 3 × 10⁸ m/s.

exam.q: How are wave speed, frequency and wavelength related?
exam.a: In one period T the wave moves forward one wavelength, so v = λ / T = λf. At a fixed speed f ∝ 1/λ: a higher frequency means a shorter wavelength. Intensity is a separate idea: I ∝ A², so doubling the amplitude gives 4 × the intensity.

exam.q: Define infrasound, audible sound and ultrasound.
exam.a: Infrasound has frequencies below 20 Hz, audible sound (the range of human hearing) is 20 Hz to 20 000 Hz, and ultrasound is above 20 000 Hz. Medical ultrasound uses frequencies in the MHz range, millions of hertz.

exam.q: Why does medical imaging use ultrasound rather than audible sound?
exam.a: Ultrasound has a very high frequency and so, at the same speed in tissue, a very short wavelength (v = λf). Short wavelengths resolve small structures, and the sound is above hearing, so it can be sent into the body and its echoes used to build an image.

exam.q: How does the ultrasound frequency chosen relate to the depth being imaged?
exam.a: Higher MHz frequencies give finer detail but are absorbed faster, so they suit superficial structures (e.g. 10–15 MHz for thyroid, breast, musculoskeletal). Lower frequencies reach deeper organs with less detail. So frequency trades detail against depth.

shockWaves.title: Shock waves, Mach number and ESWL

exam.q: Define a shock wave and the Mach number.
exam.a: A shock wave is the cone-shaped, very large-amplitude wave front formed when a source moves faster than the speed of sound (vₛ > v), with the source at the tip of the cone. The Mach number is Ma = vₛ / v, how many times faster than sound the source moves.

exam.q: Why is a sonic boom heard when a shock wave reaches you?
exam.a: A supersonic source outruns its own wave fronts, so the fronts pile up along the edge of a cone instead of spreading ahead of it. That piled-up front has an unusually large pressure amplitude, and its sudden arrival at the ear is heard as a sonic boom.

exam.q: How are shock waves used to treat kidney stones (ESWL)?
exam.a: Extracorporeal shock wave lithotripsy makes strong, short, high-pressure pulses outside the body. They pass in through a water cushion or gel and are focused on the stone, found by X-ray or ultrasound. Many shocks break it into small pieces that leave in the urine, with no skin incision.

zerothLaw.title: The zeroth law of thermodynamics
points: **Thermal equilibrium** means the bodies are at the **same temperature**, so **no net heat flows** between them.
A **conducting wall** lets heat pass, so two bodies touching through it reach the same temperature; an **insulating wall** blocks heat, so they cannot.

The law makes **temperature** a meaningful, measurable quantity: any body (a thermometer) that is in equilibrium with A and with B tells us A and B are at the same temperature **without** them touching.

**Clinical link:** a clinical thermometer is left in contact with the patient until it stops changing — that is, until it is in thermal equilibrium — and only then is its reading the patient's temperature.

exam.q: State the zeroth law of thermodynamics.
exam.a: If bodies A and B are each in thermal equilibrium with a third body T, then A and B are in thermal equilibrium with each other. Thermal equilibrium means they are at the same temperature, so no heat flows between them.

exam.q: Why does nothing happen when A and B are finally allowed to touch?
exam.a: T showed the same reading against A and against B, so A and B were already at the same temperature. Heat only flows from a hotter to a colder body, so with no temperature difference no heat flows and nothing changes when the insulating wall is removed.

exam.q: How does the zeroth law relate to measuring a patient's temperature?
exam.a: The thermometer plays the part of body T: it is held in contact until it reaches thermal equilibrium with the patient, so it is at the patient's temperature and its reading can be trusted. Without the law, a thermometer reading would not tell us anything about another body.

temperature.title: Temperature scales, triple point and the phase diagram

exam.q: Define the triple point of water.
exam.a: The triple point is the single temperature and pressure at which solid ice, liquid water and water vapour all coexist in equilibrium. For water it is 273.16 K (0.01 °C) at about 611.657 Pa, about 0.6 kPa.

exam.q: Why is the triple point used as a fixed point rather than the normal boiling point?
exam.a: Boiling and freezing points shift with pressure: water boils at 100 °C only at 1 atm. The triple point happens at only one temperature and one pressure, so it is exactly reproducible and is used to define the Kelvin scale.

exam.q: How are the Kelvin, Celsius and Fahrenheit scales related?
exam.a: T(K) = T(°C) + 273.15 and T(°F) = 9/5 T(°C) + 32. So body temperature 37 °C = 310.15 K = 98.6 °F, water freezes at 0 °C = 273.15 K = 32 °F, and absolute zero is 0 K = −273.15 °C = −459.67 °F.

exam.q: Define a simple magnifier.
exam.a: A simple magnifier is a convex lens of short focal length used to give a magnified image of a small object. The object is placed between the optical centre and the focus F, giving a virtual, erect, magnified image on the same side as the object.

exam.q: Why must the object be inside the focal length of the lens?
exam.a: Inside F the rays leave the lens diverging, so they never meet on the far side: the eye traces them back to a virtual, upright, enlarged image. At F the rays come out parallel and no image forms; beyond F the lens makes a real, inverted image instead.

exam.q: How is the angular magnification related to the focal length?
exam.a: M = θ / θ₀ = 25 cm / f, with the image at the near point N = 25 cm. A shorter focal length gives a higher magnification. It is used to examine skin lesions, in dental inspection and to read small medical scales and labels.

exam.q: Define the objective and the eyepiece of a compound microscope.
exam.a: The objective is the convex lens nearest the specimen, with a very short focal length (fₒ < 1 cm), which forms the first, real magnified image I₁. The eyepiece is a convex lens of a few centimetres focal length (fₑ > fₒ) that acts as a simple magnifier on I₁.

exam.q: Why is the final image of a compound microscope inverted?
exam.a: The objective forms a real, inverted image I₁ of the object. The eyepiece, used as a simple magnifier, makes a virtual image of I₁ the same way up as I₁. So the final image I₂ stays inverted relative to the original object.

exam.q: How do the two lenses work together to give high magnification?
exam.a: The object sits just outside Fₒ, so the objective makes an enlarged real image I₁ at or just inside Fₑ; the eyepiece then magnifies I₁ again into a virtual image. The total magnification is the product of the two, which is why it is used for blood cells, histopathology and microbiology.
